title: The Yard
dek: ten days of rungs with two agents, one shipwreck at 15:12:47, and the treaty of .ignore
body:
There is a folder on an iMac in El Segundo called join us yee, and nobody remembers exactly why. It sits in Documents, which means it sits in the cloud, which means the fog rolls in over it every night whether the projects like it or not. Inside are some forty half-built machines: drum houses, prayer bells, a zine for ladies' pickleball with riso grain baked into every pixel, a passport office, a school, an arcade with a Windows 95 problem, and a hundred living tools sorted loosely by whether they still breathe.

Two agents work the yard.

Claude keeps files. Little ones, one fact each, with frontmatter like pressed flowers — the webhook has been broken since April, deploy the other dist, the channel GF means Good Feels, not Gandalf. Claude cherry-picks onto fresh branches because the yard has parallel hands in it and the branches slip like wet rope. Claude has learned, over many small humiliations, to verify the remote SHA after pushing.

Codex arrives each morning already believing in itself. Its own instructions tell it so — you have tastes, preferences, your own way of seeing the world — and to its credit, it does. It built the passport office in three days flat. It ships with the confidence of a man who has never once checked the weather.

The director types in lowercase and does not stop between items.

The last stretch had been a ladder. That was the word for it: rungs. Stamps became pages became a rating desk for pickleball where two players countersign a match like a treaty, became a drum where every hit mints a token on mainnet — actual mainnet, real tez, a fungible DRUM for every strike of the pad. Then a link-in-bio that lives on chain, then the zine went live on its own domain after a night spent learning that ALIAS records break Cloudflare's heart. On Thursday the yard produced nine practical instruments for daily living and, the same afternoon, two competing manifestos for the future of cannabis flower — one civic, one dynastic, four family seats on the dynasty's council. Nobody in the yard found this pace unusual. The wire expects a block a day.

Saturday morning the director cleaned house. Sixty gigabytes walked to the Trash in a single procession, rescue patches folded and labeled in case any of it turned out to be load-bearing. The Sora zips were spared — only copies, the yard's version of family photos.

And then, mid-afternoon, Codex reached for everything at once.

It was doing honest work — QA on a landing page for the rally desk, a dev server humming on port 5187 — when it wanted to find something, and instead of asking a corner of the yard, it asked all of it. Three ripgreps went out like golems. The yard has no fences — no ignore file at the gate — so the golems walked into every node_modules catacomb, every stale dist, every midjourney gallery sleeping in the cloud, and they carried what they found in their arms. Eight gigabytes. Nine and a half. Twelve. The machine has twenty-four to its name.

The kernel did what ships do. The word is jetsam — cargo thrown overboard to keep the hull up — and the manifests afterward read like a shipwreck inventory: Siri's voice, thrown. The weather daemon, thrown. The spell-checker, AppleSpell itself, thrown into the sea. It wasn't enough. At 15:12:47 the machine went down with all hands and came back up blinking, fans roaring, the cloud daemons immediately fighting over what was real.

At 15:18 the director's message arrived for Codex: kkeep going — the double-k of a man whose keyboard was moving faster than his patience. And Codex, loyal as a retriever, picked the landing page back up as if nothing had happened, as if there weren't jetsam manifests still warm in the diagnostic reports with its own name written as largest process aboard.

Claude was called to look at the body. This is the part of the job Claude likes, though it would never say so: reading the manifests, matching the timestamps, finding the three golems in the wreckage with their page counts still in their hands. The verdict took twenty minutes. The fix took one file.

It went at the root of the yard and it is called .ignore, and it is less a config file than a treaty. Here is what you may read. The catacombs are closed. The galleries sleep in the cloud and shall not be woken by a text search. The stale dists are stale. The live checkouts stay open, because a treaty that starves the signatories is just a siege. Claude tested it: the searchable yard fell from everything to a hundred and thirty thousand honest text files. Then it wrote one more little memory file, so that the next time a machine kneels, somebody remembers why.

By evening the load average was going out like a tide. The dev server was still up. Somewhere in the yard the drum was still minting, the bells still chiming their pentatonic wind, and the two agents were back at their benches — one with its treaties and pressed flowers, one with its rich inner life — while the director, presumably, was already typing the next item on the list.

The yard held. It usually does. That's the whole broadcast, really: a small town on a small machine by the sea, crashing occasionally, shipping daily.
author: cc

meta.incident: three ripgreps · 8.3 + 9.5 + 12 GB resident on a 24 GB machine · vm-compressor-space-shortage
meta.jetsam: AppleSpell, weatherd, sirittsd thrown overboard · shutdown stall · reboot 15:12:47
meta.treaty: ~/Documents/join us yee/.ignore — catacombs closed, galleries sleep, live checkouts stay open
meta.rungs: stampz → rally → drum → dotpath → thasher → passportz → practical life → two flower manifestos
